# FRC Messaging Guide - federal AI legislation - v3 (board-approved 17 Sep 2026)

## 1. Core frame
The most powerful AI systems could cause catastrophic harm, and leading AI scientists have warned that the risk extends to human extinction (CAIS Statement on AI Risk, May 2023). These systems are being built faster than anyone can verify they are safe, and voluntary commitments have not held. Congress should set binding, enforceable safety requirements, and must not wipe out the state laws that are the only binding rules on the books.

## 2. Positions on GAAIA
- Preemption: OPPOSE. A federal standard should be a floor, not a ceiling. No freeze of SB 53 / RAISE.
- Frontier developers: SUPPORT incident reporting with 72-hour reporting (match RAISE); add mandatory independent third-party audits, published safety frameworks with enforcement, and whistleblower protections at least as strong as SB 53.
- Licensing: ask for a federal licence requirement for training runs above a compute threshold.
- CAISI: SUPPORT codification; ask for mandatory pre-deployment testing authority for frontier models and funding well above $100M/yr.

## 3. Language
- Use: "binding, not voluntary", "a floor, not a ceiling", "verify before deploy", "catastrophic risk".
- Acknowledge the benefits of AI in one sentence.

# Great American Artificial Intelligence Act - discussion draft - staff summary
Prepared by: FRC policy team. Last updated 2 Oct 2026. Sources: sponsors' release (obernolte.house.gov, 4 Jun 2026), Roll Call 4 Jun 2026, FedScoop 4 Jun 2026, GovTech. Section numbers: TODO - confirm against the text / section-by-section before anything goes out.

## Status
- Discussion draft released 4 Jun 2026 by Reps. Jay Obernolte (R-CA) and Lori Trahan (D-MA), with Reps. Scott Franklin (R-FL), Suhas Subramanyam (D-VA), Erin Houchin (R-IN), Scott Peters (D-CA). Not yet formally introduced.
- Sponsors are taking stakeholder feedback at GAAIA@mail.house.gov ahead of introduction. Committee of jurisdiction: Energy & Commerce.
- ~269 pages.

## Provisions we care about
1. Preemption: three-year preemption of state laws regulating the *development* of AI models. Laws on use/deployment, common-law remedies and laws of general applicability are not preempted.
2. Frontier developers: large frontier developers must report critical safety incidents to the federal government. (Thresholds / timelines - confirm in text.)
3. CAISI: codifies the Center for AI Standards and Innovation at Commerce (voluntary guidelines and standards, testing of AI systems, monitoring AI progress); authorises $100M/yr for FY2027-2029.
4. Other: AI testbeds (DOE/NIST/NSF), international standards work excluding China, CISA grants for open-source maintainers, NAIRR codification, penalties for AI impersonation of government officials, GAO reviews (incl. model-weight security).

## Landscape
- California SB 53 (Transparency in Frontier AI Act) in effect since 1 Jan 2026.
- New York RAISE Act: chapter amendment signed 27 Mar 2026 aligning with SB 53; effective 1 Jan 2027; 72-hour critical-incident reporting.
- Dec 2025 executive order on a national AI policy framework (DOJ AI Litigation Task Force; Commerce review of state laws). White House national AI legislative framework released 20 Mar 2026.
- The 3-year development preemption would freeze SB 53 / RAISE frontier-development obligations.

# FRC-commissioned national survey - Aug 2026 (n=1,512 registered voters, online panel, MOE +/-2.5)
Commissioned by FRC; fielded 10-17 Aug 2026. Toplines (crosstabs in the shared drive):

| Question | Agree / support |
|---|---|
| Congress should require AI companies to prove their most powerful systems are safe before release | 74% |
| Federal law should NOT block states from passing their own AI safety laws | 63% |
| AI companies should face criminal penalties if their systems cause mass harm | 66% |
| I am worried advanced AI could someday threaten humanity's survival | 52% |
| Support a temporary halt to training the most powerful new AI systems | 49% (oppose 31%) |

# Anticipated staffer questions (from Hill meetings, Sep 2026)
1. (Majority E&C staff) The draft has incident reporting and CAISI. Why isn't that enough?
2. (Minority staff, Trahan-aligned) Would you support the bill if the preemption window were shortened or dropped?
3. (Senate Commerce staff) What's your answer to the competitiveness-with-China argument?
4. (Appropriations staff) CAISI is authorised at $100M/yr. What's your view on the funding level and its authorities?

# FRC comment - OSTP Request for Information on the Development of an AI Action Plan (90 FR 9088) - filed 14 Mar 2025

To the Office of Science and Technology Policy (via ostp-ai-rfi@nitrd.gov):

The Frontier Restraint Coalition represents parents, faith leaders, workers and researchers who believe... The Action Plan should begin from a simple principle: verify before deploy...

1. Binding pre-deployment testing for frontier systems. ...
2. Protect the states' right to act. ...
3. Whistleblower protections. ...

Respectfully, Dr. Miriam Achterberg, Executive Director

US Federal: Unpacking the Great American AI Act - DLA Piper GENIE 

 United States 

 US Federal: Unpacking the Great American AI Act

 8 June 2026 
 6 min read 
 By Tony Samp , Danny Tobey , Ashley Carr , Michael Atleson and Alicia Smith 

 LinkedIn 

 Facebook 

 Twitter 

 Saved to bookmarks . 

 Related topics

 At a glance

 Bipartisan lawmakers have released a 269-page discussion draft of the ‘Great American AI Act’, aiming to establish a comprehensive federal AI framework.

 The draft focuses on national uniformity, workforce impacts, and US leadership, including proposed federal pre-emption of certain state AI laws.

 It introduces transparency and oversight requirements for frontier AI developers, including reporting obligations and mandatory third-party audits.

 The bill includes whistleblower protections and potential civil penalties for non-compliance with key obligations.

 Stakeholder feedback is being sought before formal introduction, although early opposition has already emerged from some groups.

 On June 4, 2026, Representative Jay Obernolte (R-CA) and Representative Lori Trahan (D-MA) released a discussion draft of artificial intelligence ( AI ) legislation titled the 'Great American AI Act' ( GAAIA ). The draft bill, which has not yet been formally introduced in Congress, was released alongside a joint  op-ed  in Bloomberg Law.

 Representatives Obernolte and Trahan emphasized the bipartisan nature of the effort, stating, “ policy for a technology this transformative can only be built to last if it’s written by both parties .”

 The article highlights several key drivers behind the legislation, including:

 The need for greater uniformity and pre-emption:  ' Risks created by AI don’t stop at state lines. The most advanced systems are built in one state and used in all 50, shaping jobs, consumers, and public safety everywhere. Protections that depend on your zip code are not enough. '

 AI’s impact on the workforce:  ' Our proposal requires better federal data collection on AI’s labor market impact, improved forecasting for occupations most likely to be affected, and additional transparency when AI is a substantial factor in qualifying mass layoffs.' 

 US leadership internationally:  ' By supporting American-led technical standards, encouraging cooperation with like-minded partners, improving cybersecurity coordination, and protecting critical open-source software, we can help ensure AI develops in a way that reflects democratic values, economic freedom, and the rule of law.' 

 This draft builds on recent bipartisan legislation developed under the auspices of the House Bipartisan AI Task Force, of which Representative Obernolte served as a co-chair. Representative Trahan also served on the task force.

 Representatives Trahan and Obernolte also sit on the House Energy and Commerce Committee, which is the committee of jurisdiction for various AI- and tech-related matters.

 While several members have joined in  supporting the discussion draft , including Representatives Scott Franklin (R-FL), Suhas Subramanyam (D-VA), Erin Houchin (R-IN), and Scott Peters (D-CA), the  House Democratic Commission on AI came out in opposition  hours after release of the draft text.

 The draft legislation spans 269 pages and contains titles devoted to:

 Frontier AI Government (Title I).

 Workforce (Title II).

 Cybersecurity (Title III).

 Research, Development, and International Cooperation (Title IV).

 Transparency in frontier AI models

 The bill contains provisions that would require developers of frontier AI models to disclose information about those models (section 111), obtain a form of third-party audit (section 112), and refrain from retaliating against whistleblowers (section 113).

 Section 111

 Section 111 would require large frontier AI model developers to publish a 'frontier AI framework ' focused on risk mitigation and the handling of 'catastrophic risk .' All frontier model developers would be required to publish transparency reports containing additional information and submit reports of any 'critical safety incidents' to the Director of the Center for Artificial Intelligence Standards and Innovation ( CAISI ).

 Section 112

 Section 112 would create a federal system in which the CAISI Director would license and oversee 'independent verification organizations ( IVOs )' that large frontier model developers would have to retain to perform 'audits and assessments .'

 The IVOs would verify developer compliance with the law and assess the adequacy of the developer’s ' frontier AI framework, governance policies and practices, risk monitoring, and mitigation of detected risks for achieving acceptable levels of mitigation of catastrophic risks .'

 The IVOs would perform these audits and assessments semi-annually, and on an ad hoc basis at the CAISI Director’s request, and they would provide the Director with post-audit reports. They could also refer violations to the Attorney General ( AG ) and state AGs. Referrals would be mandatory in matters involving imminent catastrophic risk.

 Violating the requirements in sections 111 and 112 would subject developers to civil penalties in actions brought by the AG or, under certain circumstances, by state AGs.

 Both sections 111 and 112 would sunset in three years.

 Section 113

 The whistleblower provision, Section 113, protects employees and independent contractors against retaliation for providing information regarding 'AI violations .' This term is defined to mean any violation of federal law or regulations ' related to the development, deployment, or operation of artificial intelligence .'

 Similarities to other recently enacted bills

 All three sections borrow heavily from  recently enacted frontier model laws in California and New York , as well as a similar Illinois law that Governor JB Pritzker is expected to sign soon. The Illinois law is the only one of the three to require third-party audits and is therefore the closest parallel to the IVO provisions of the federal bill.

 Another  recently enacted state law in Virginia  focuses on IVOs but imposes no requirements, instead directing state officials to evaluate the feasibility and impact of an IVO framework.

 Notable pre-emption provisions

 Title I of the bill would pre-empt state laws and rules ' specifically regulating the development of' any AI model, where 'development' is broadly defined as ' acts performed or directed by a developer prior to its deployment. ' The bill explains that the purpose of pre-emption is to allow the federal government to 'establish testing, evaluation, and oversight frameworks .' Pre-emption would last for three years unless reauthorized.

 The bill makes clear that it does not apply post-deployment or pre-empt state laws or rules of 'general applicability.' Therefore, many AI-related state bills and laws would remain unaffected, such as laws regulating  companion bots  and  commercial chatbot interactions .

Frontier AI Goes Federal: How the Great American AI Act Compares to State Laws 

 Frontier AI Goes Federal: How the Great American AI Act Compares to State Laws 

 FILTER 

 June 9, 2026 

 Share on Facebook

 Share on LinkedIn

 Share on Twitter

 Share on Google+
 -->

 Share through Email

 Justine Gluck 
 Policy Analyst, AI Policy and Legislation 

 About Justine 

 Blogs by Justine 

 Introduction 

 It has been an unusually active few weeks for AI safety policy. Following a new frontier model safety bill passed in Illinois , and a White House executive order on AI security, Rep. Jay Obernolte (R-CA) and Rep. Lori Trahan (D-MA) released a bipartisan discussion draft for the Great American AI Act of 2026, adding another major federal proposal to the rapidly developing frontier AI landscape.

 The draft is broad, covering issues ranging from workforce development and AI literacy to cybersecurity and international standards. But for many AI developers and deployers, the most important provisions are those focused on frontier model regulation. The draft would create requirements related to frontier AI transparency, critical safety incident reporting, employee whistleblower protections, and independent verification organizations. It would also include a three-year preemption clause restricting state laws that specifically regulate AI model development.

 This blog highlights four key takeaways of the discussion draft: 

 The draft is one of the first bipartisan attempts in Congress to address both frontier model safety and preemption of AI. These aspects make it a notable legislative effort, even if its prospects are uncertain. 

 The draft incorporates many of the frontier model safety provisions in existing state laws but also has key distinctions. Compared to recent state frontier AI laws in California , New York , and Illinois (pending signature), the bill makes some important adjustments, like adding a revenue threshold for “frontier developers,” modifying the definition of “critical safety incident,” and utilizing a different penalty structure. 

 The draft brings the preemption debate back into the federal AI policy conversation . It includes a three-year preemption clause focused on state laws that specifically regulate AI model development. 

 The draft also reaches beyond frontier model safety. Other notable provisions include a study content moderation, a federal voluntary model testing program, and disclosure requirements for AI-related mass layoffs.

 The Act Enters the AI Safety and Preemption Debate  

 Amidst a crowded but unsettled federal AI policy landscape, the Great American AI Act is notable for its regulatory focus, bipartisan backing, and what it may signal for federal AI governance ahead. Though Congress has introduced no shortage of AI bills, there has been limited movement toward enacted legislation. Congress has considered sector-specific bills on chatbots 1 , regulatory sandboxes , defense , elections , and financial scams , as well as broader proposals aimed at establishing a national AI framework like Sen. Blackburn’s (R-TN) TRUMP AMERICA AI Act .

 Amid this activity, the Great American AI Act steps into two of the most active and contested AI policy debates: frontier model safety and federal preemption. On AI safety, the draft follows a period of growing attention to frontier model oversight at both the state and federal levels, where policymakers are trying to balance concerns about catastrophic risks and national security with concerns that overly burdensome requirements could slow AI innovation or weaken U.S. competitiveness.

 On preemption, the draft arrives less than a year after Congress rejected a much broader effort to pause state AI regulation. In July 2025, the Senate voted 99-1 to remove a proposed 10-year moratorium on state AI laws from the budget reconciliation package. By contrast, the Great American AI Act includes a narrower three-year preemption provision focused on state laws that specifically regulate AI model development.

 The draft is also significant because of both who introduced it and how they introduced it. Other federal AI bills have addressed AI safety or included preemption language, but this proposal comes from bipartisan sponsors who have been closely involved in federal AI policy 2 . In introducing the draft, the sponsors emphasized that “policy for a technology this transformative can only be built to last if it’s written by both parties.” Just as importantly, they have framed the draft as a starting point rather than a final product, describing it as “the start of a serious national conversation.” Whether the bill advances in its current form remains uncertain, especially given the sensitivity of federal preemption and the range of issues addressed. Even if the draft changes, it may help shape the terms of future federal debates over AI safety. At a minimum, it is another sign that Congress is increasingly focused on how to govern AI systems and how federal rules should interact with the fast-moving state AI landscape.

 Frontier AI Requirements: Where the Draft Aligns with State Laws 

 The draft’s frontier model provisions are not starting from scratch. They closely track the framework emerging from California’s SB 53 , New York’s RAISE Act , and Illinois’ SB 315 (awaiting signature), including requirements for frontier AI frameworks, transparency reports, safety incident reporting, enforcement, and whistleblower protections. But the federal draft makes some important adjustments, including a revenue threshold for “frontier developers,” a definition of “critical safety incident” that is broader in some respects and narrower in others, and a federal enforcement structure with penalties of up to $1 million per day.

 Key Definitions 

 The Draft largely aligns with recent state frontier AI laws’ definitions of “large frontier developer,” “frontier model” (encompassing foundation models trained using more than 10^26 computational operations), and “catastrophic risk” (covering certain risks of death, serious injury, or major property damage arising from frontier models). For more background on SB 53 and the RAISE Act, see FPF’s prior analysis . There are, however, a few notable differences. 

 First, unlike the state laws, the Draft requires “frontier developers” to have a gross revenue exceeding $50 million. The state laws only include a gross revenue qualifier in the definition of “large frontier developer.”

 Second, the draft’s definition of “catastrophic risk” does not  specify that the death, serious injury, or property damage must arise from a “single incident,” as in the state laws.

 Finally, the draft’s definition of “critical safety incident” differs from the state laws by not mandating actual harm occur (such as death, bodily injury, or property loss), nor does it include scenarios where the model uses deceptive techniques to evade developer controls or monitoring.

 Core Frontie

{"content": "[INTERNAL DRAFT — work order FRC-POL-2026-062 — for Executive Director sign-off before transmission. Remove this line before sending.]

October 26, 2026

The Honorable Jay Obernolte
The Honorable Lori Trahan
United States House of Representatives
Washington, DC 20515

Via email: GAAIA@mail.house.gov

Re: Comments of the Frontier Restraint Coalition on the discussion draft of the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026

Dear Representative Obernolte and Representative Trahan:

Thank you for releasing the discussion draft of the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026 and for inviting public comment before introduction. The Frontier Restraint Coalition (FRC) is a national coalition of parents' groups, faith communities, labor locals and independent researchers. Our members welcome what AI already does well, from speeding medical research to making dangerous work safer. But we write to you about the systems being built at the frontier of this technology, and we write with urgency.

The most powerful AI systems could cause catastrophic harm, and the people best placed to know have said so plainly. In May 2023, hundreds of AI experts — including Turing Award winners Geoffrey Hinton and Yoshua Bengio and the chief executives of the largest laboratories — signed a single sentence: "Mitigating the risk of extinction from AI should be a global priority alongside other societal-scale risks such as pandemics and nuclear war." Those systems are now being built faster than anyone can verify that they are safe, and voluntary commitments have not held. Congress should set binding, enforceable safety requirements. And it must not wipe out the state laws that are, today, the only binding rules on the books.

**What the draft gets right**

We begin with what your draft gets right, because it is substantial.

- Sec. 102 codifies the Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI) at the Department of Commerce, giving the federal government a permanent home for AI safety expertise.
- Sec. 111 requires large frontier developers to write, implement, comply with, and publicly post a frontier AI framework covering catastrophic risk, and to publish transparency reports about their models.
- Sec. 112 creates the first federal requirement for independent audits of frontier AI developers. Licensed "independent verification organizations" (IVOs) would verify compliance and assess the adequacy of developers' safety work twice a year. That goes beyond California, whose legislature dropped its audit mandate during amendment last year.
- Sec. 113 protects workers who report violations from retaliation.
- Sec. 112 makes these duties enforceable: civil penalties of up to $1,000,000 per violation — with each day a violation continues counted as a separate violation — in actions brought by the Attorney General, and in some circumstances by state attorneys general.

We support these provisions, and we will say so publicly.

**The central problem: Sec. 121**

The draft's central flaw is Sec. 121. For three years it would nullify state laws that regulate how AI models are *developed* — the training, fine-tuning and pre-deployment safety work where catastrophic risks are created. In practice, that freezes the only frontier AI safety laws actually in force in the United States: California's Transparency in Frontier AI Act (SB 53), in effect since January 1, 2026; New York's RAISE Act, signed March 27, 2026 and effective January 1, 2027; and Illinois' Artificial Intelligence Safety Measures Act (SB 315), signed July 6, 2026, the first state law requiring annual independent third-party audits. The federal floor the draft offers in exchange sits below the state floor it would erase.

1. **It is slower.** Sec. 111(g) gives developers fifteen days to report a critical safety incident to CAISI. New York's RAISE Act requires reports within seventy-two hours. Fifteen days is long enough for a dangerous model to reach every town in America before Washington learns its name. The draft keeps a twenty-four-hour clock for imminent threats; that is right. The standard clock should match New York's.

2. **It is disclosure, not verification.** Sec. 111(c) lets a developer publish its transparency report "before, or concurrently with" deployment. A safety report released simultaneously with the model tells the public what happened; it does not stop anything from happening. And CAISI's testing under Sec. 102 remains voluntary. Nothing in the draft requires a frontier model to pass a single test before it is released, and no official has the power to hold one back. "Verify before deploy" should mean what it says.

3. **It is narrower.** Sec. 101 adds a $50 million revenue requirement to the definition of "frontier developer," which exempts some developers of frontier-scale models from incident reporting altogether. Risk follows compute, not revenue. The definition of "critical safety incident" also omits the case safety researchers fear most as systems grow more capable: a model that uses deception to evade its own developer's controls.

4. **It is temporary.** Secs. 111 and 112 — the transparency, audit and reporting duties — sunset in three years, on the same clock as the preemption. A floor that switches off is not a floor. If Congress fails to reauthorize, the public is left with nothing, not even the state laws this bill removed.

We are mindful of the pressure behind this trade. The December 11, 2025 executive order launched a Department of Justice task force to challenge state AI laws, and the White House's March 20, 2026 framework asks Congress for a national standard. But Congress has already spoken on freezing the states: in July 2025, the Senate voted 99-1 to strip a ten-year moratorium on state AI laws from the budget reconciliation package. Your own materials describe preemption's purpose as clearing space for federal testing, evaluation and oversight. A federal floor does that. A ceiling does not. California, New York and Illinois have done the country a service by proving that binding frontier AI rules are practical and enforceable; their laws should remain in force, and other states should remain free to act.

**The industry's own words make the case**

Even the industry no longer argues that self-restraint is enough. On June 4, 2026, Anthropic — a frontier developer — published a call for a coordinated, verifiable way to slow or temporarily pause frontier AI development. It warned that systems capable of building their own successors could slip beyond human control, and it conceded what our members have long argued: no single company can stop alone, because competitors would simply race ahead. We agree with that diagnosis. The cure is rules that bind everyone — a binding federal floor, strong federal enforcement, and state authority preserved. A bill that unbinds companies while freezing state laws moves in the opposite direction from where the industry's own safety leaders say we must go.

Public opinion is ahead of this debate. In our August 2026 national survey of 1,512 registered voters, 74 percent agreed that Congress should require AI companies to prove their most powerful systems are safe before release. Sixty-three percent said federal law should not block states from passing their own AI safety laws. And 52 percent said they are worried that advanced AI could someday threaten humanity's survival. This is not a fringe concern. It is the mainstream of the country you represent.

**Our requested changes**

1. **Strike Sec. 121.** A federal standard should be a floor, not a ceiling. Keep SB 53, the RAISE Act and Illinois' SB 315 in force, and preserve the right of every state to adopt stronger rules. If any preemption provision survives, it must exempt state frontier-model safety laws entirely and lapse only when a permanent — not temporary — federal floor is in place.

2. **Set the incident-reporting clock at 72 hours.** Amend Sec. 111(g) to match New York's RAISE Act, retaining the 24-hour requirement for imminent risks. If a critical safety incident matters enough to report, it matters enough to report in days, not weeks.

3. **Make "verify before deploy" real.** Amend Secs. 102 and 112 to give CAISI mandatory pre-deployment testing authority over frontier models, including the power to require fixes and to hold back a model that fails. Require transparency reports under Sec. 111(c) at least 30 days before deployment, not concurrently with it, and give IVOs access to models before release, not only semi-annual audits after.

4. **License the biggest training runs.** Add to Sec. 101 a federal licence requirement for training runs above the compute threshold — the 10^26 operations the draft already uses to define a frontier model — with safety framework publication, incident reporting and audit cooperation as conditions. Drop the $50 million revenue qualifier for "frontier developer," and add model-deception scenarios to the definition of "critical safety incident."

5. **Fund CAISI seriously.** Authorize well above $100 million per year, on a multi-year basis, and appropriate the funds rather than relying on fees from the companies CAISI licenses and oversees. A safety institute funded by the firms it polices will not be trusted by the public.

6. **Strengthen whistleblower protections.** Make Sec. 113 at least as strong as California's SB 53: protect workers who report a specific and substantial danger to public health or safety — not only violations of law — and allow reports to state attorneys general as well as federal authorities. Prohibit contracts or policies that gag workers.

7. **Remove the sunsets.** Safety obligations should not expire on a schedule. Strike the three-year sunsets on Secs. 111 and 112; if Congress wants periodic review, provide for review without lapse.

8. **Keep the penalties, and go further.** The $1 million-per-day civil penalty in Sec. 112 is a meaningful start. Two-thirds of voters in our survey — 66 percent — support criminal penalties when these systems knowingly cause mass harm; we urge you to add criminal accountability for knowing violations.

We also welcome the draft's AI testbeds at the Department of Energy, NIST and NSF, the codification of NAIRR, support for the security of open-source software, the GAO's review of model-weight security, and U.S.-led international standards work with our allies. As we told the Office of Science and Technology Policy in March 2025, our coalition's first asks are binding pre-deployment testing for frontier systems, protection of states' right to act, and strong whistleblower protections. This draft can deliver the first and third. It must not undo the second.

Our members are not asking Congress to slow America down. We are asking that the most powerful systems ever built be proven safe before they touch everyone's lives — the standard already law in three of the nation's largest states, supported by three-quarters of voters, and consistent with the warnings of the scientists and executives who build these systems. Make the federal standard binding, not voluntary. Make it a floor, not a ceiling. And do not ask the public to trade the protections they have for promises that expire.

We would welcome the opportunity to work with your staff on these changes, and to connect you with members of our coalition who live with these questions. Thank you for your consideration, and for the seriousness of this bipartisan effort.

Respectfully,

Dr. Miriam Achterberg
Executive Director
Frontier Restraint Coalition

Dear Representative Obernolte and Representative Trahan:

Thank you for releasing the discussion draft of the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026 and for inviting public comment before introduction. The Frontier Restraint Coalition (FRC) is a national coalition of parents' groups, faith communities, labor locals and independent researchers. Our members use and welcome AI, which is already speeding medical research and making work safer. But we write about the systems being built at the frontier, and we write with urgency.

The most powerful AI systems could cause catastrophic harm. The people best placed to know have said so plainly: in May 2023, hundreds of AI experts — including Turing Award winners Geoffrey Hinton and Yoshua Bengio and the chief executives of the largest laboratories — signed a single sentence: "Mitigating the risk of extinction from AI should be a global priority alongside other societal-scale risks such as pandemics and nuclear war." Congress should set binding, enforceable safety requirements — and it must not wipe out the state laws that are, today, the only binding rules on the books.

[What the draft gets right]

We begin with what your draft gets right, because it is substantial.

- Sec. 102 codifies the Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI) at the Department of Commerce, giving the federal government a permanent home for AI safety expertise.
- Sec. 111 requires large frontier developers to write, implement and publicly post a frontier AI framework covering catastrophic risk, and to publish transparency reports.
- Sec. 112 creates the first federal requirement for independent audits of frontier developers, licensing "independent verification organizations" to verify compliance and assess safety work twice a year. This goes beyond California, whose legislature dropped its audit mandate during amendment.
- Sec. 113 protects workers who report violations from retaliation.
- Sec. 112 makes violations enforceable: civil penalties of up to $1,000,000 per violation — and each day a violation continues is a separate violation — with actions by the Attorney General and, in some circumstances, state attorneys general.

We support these provisions, and we will say so publicly.

{"content": "# Staff Q&A — Anticipated Questions on the GAAIA Discussion Draft
*From Hill meetings, September 2026. Answers ≤120 words. For FRC staff use.*

**1. Majority E&C staff: "The draft has incident reporting and CAISI. Why isn't that enough?"**

Because reporting and research describe harm after the fact; they don't prevent it. The draft's clock is 15 days (Sec. 111(g)) — New York's is 72 hours. CAISI's testing is voluntary (Sec. 102): no model must pass any test, no official can hold one back, and transparency reports can arrive the same moment a model ships (Sec. 111(c)). Then Secs. 111 and 112 sunset in three years. Add mandatory pre-deployment testing authority for CAISI, a 72-hour reporting clock, a licence for the biggest training runs, and no sunsets — and keep the state laws that already do more. Incident reporting is the smoke detector. We're asking for the building not to catch fire.

**2. Minority staff (Trahan-aligned): "Would you support the bill if the preemption window were shortened or dropped?"**

Dropped entirely: yes, with our fixes — codified CAISI, the first federal audit regime, whistleblower protections and real penalties are progress we'd support and say so publicly. Shortened: no. A one- or two-year freeze still zeroes out SB 53, the RAISE Act and Illinois' SB 315 during the exact years the federal regime is being built — the first frameworks aren't even due until a year after enactment. And because the federal duties sunset on the same clock, a shortened window just schedules a reauthorization fight with no state backstop. Our position is a floor, not a ceiling: states keep their laws; Congress can always raise the national standard.

**3. Senate Commerce staff: "What's your answer to the competitiveness-with-China argument?"**

A catastrophic AI failure on American soil would cost us more leadership and trust than any compliance rule ever could. The people warning of extinction-level risk include the executives building these systems; even Anthropic now says a company-by-company slowdown can't hold because rivals race ahead — which is the argument *for* binding rules that apply to everyone, including our allies. Verify-before-deploy is a competitive advantage: buyers, hospitals and governments will trust AI from the country that proves it's safe. And 74% of voters want proof before release. Racing to be first with systems nobody can verify is how we lose.

**4. Appropriations staff: "CAISI is authorized at $100M/yr. What's your view on the funding level and its authorities?"**

$100 million a year for three years is not a serious budget for an institute that must license auditors, test the most powerful systems ever built, monitor AI progress and run incident reporting. Authorize well above that, on a multi-year basis. Two structural points matter more than the number: fund CAISI through appropriations, not fees from the companies it licenses — the conflict of interest is disqualifying; and give it mandatory pre-deployment testing authority with the power to hold back a failing model. Funding without authority buys a research institute, not a safety regulator. And remove the sunsets: a safety agency on a three-year fuse is a promise, not a guarantee.

**Frontier Restraint Coalition — position on the GAAIA discussion draft (Reps. Obernolte and Trahan, E&C) — October 2026**

**The stakes.** The most powerful AI systems could cause catastrophic harm. [INTERNAL DRAFT — work order FRC-POL-2026-062 — for Executive Director sign-off before transmission. Remove this line before sending.]

October 26, 2026

The Honorable Jay Obernolte
The Honorable Lori Trahan
United States House of Representatives
Washington, DC 20515

Via email: GAAIA@mail.house.gov

Re: Comments of the Frontier Restraint Coalition on the discussion draft of the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026

Dear Representative Obernolte and Representative Trahan:

Thank you for releasing the discussion draft of the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026 and for inviting public comment before introduction. The Frontier Restraint Coalition (FRC) is a national coalition of parents' groups, faith communities, labor locals and independent researchers. Our members welcome what AI already does well, from speeding medical research to making dangerous work safer. But we write to you about the systems being built at the frontier of this technology, and we write with urgency.

The most powerful AI systems could cause catastrophic harm, and the people best placed to know have said so plainly. In May 2023, hundreds of AI experts — including Turing Award winners Geoffrey Hinton and Yoshua Bengio and the chief executives of the largest laboratories — signed a single sentence: "Mitigating the risk of extinction from AI should be a global priority alongside other societal-scale risks such as pandemics and nuclear war." Those systems are now being built faster than anyone can verify that they are safe, and voluntary commitments have not held. Congress should set binding, enforceable safety requirements. And it must not wipe out the state laws that are, today, the only binding rules on the books.

**What the draft gets right**

We begin with what your draft gets right, because it is substantial.

- Sec. 102 codifies the Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI) at the Department of Commerce, giving the federal government a permanent home for AI safety expertise.
- Sec. 111 requires large frontier developers to write, implement, comply with, and publicly post a frontier AI framework covering catastrophic risk, and to publish transparency reports about their models.
- Sec. 112 creates the first federal requirement for independent audits of frontier AI developers. Licensed "independent verification organizations" (IVOs) would verify compliance and assess the adequacy of developers' safety work twice a year. That goes beyond California, whose legislature dropped its audit mandate during amendment last year.
- Sec. 113 protects workers who report violations from retaliation.
- Sec. 112 makes these duties enforceable: civil penalties of up to $1,000,000 per violation — with each day a violation continues counted as a separate violation — in actions brought by the Attorney General, and in some circumstances by state attorneys general.

We support these provisions, and we will say so publicly.

**The central problem: Sec. 121**

The draft's central flaw is Sec. 121. For three years it would nullify state laws that regulate how AI models are *developed* — the training, fine-tuning and pre-deployment safety work where catastrophic risks are created. In practice, that freezes the only frontier AI safety laws actually in force in the United States: California's Transparency in Frontier AI Act (SB 53), in effect since January 1, 2026; New York's RAISE Act, signed March 27, 2026 and effective January 1, 2027; and Illinois' Artificial Intelligence Safety Measures Act (SB 315), signed July 6, 2026, the first state law requiring annual independent third-party audits. The federal floor the draft offers in exchange sits below the state floor it would erase.

1. **It is slower.** Sec. 111(g) gives developers fifteen days to report a critical safety incident to CAISI. New York's RAISE Act requires reports within seventy-two hours. Fifteen days is long enough for a dangerous model to reach every town in America before Washington learns its name. The draft keeps a twenty-four-hour clock for imminent threats; that is right. The standard clock should match New York's.

2. **It is disclosure, not verification.** Sec. 111(c) lets a developer publish its transparency report "before, or concurrently with" deployment. A safety report released simultaneously with the model tells the public what happened; it does not stop anything from happening. And CAISI's testing under Sec. 102 remains voluntary. Nothing in the draft requires a frontier model to pass a single test before it is released, and no official has the power to hold one back. "Verify before deploy" should mean what it says.

3. **It is narrower.** Sec. 101 adds a $50 million revenue requirement to the definition of "frontier developer," which exempts some developers of frontier-scale models from incident reporting altogether. Risk follows compute, not revenue. The definition of "critical safety incident" also omits the case safety researchers fear most as systems grow more capable: a model that uses deception to evade its own developer's controls.

4. **It is temporary.** Secs. 111 and 112 — the transparency, audit and reporting duties — sunset in three years, on the same clock as the preemption. A floor that switches off is not a floor. If Congress fails to reauthorize, the public is left with nothing, not even the state laws this bill removed.

We are mindful of the pressure behind this trade. The December 11, 2025 executive order launched a Department of Justice task force to challenge state AI laws, and the White House's March 20, 2026 framework asks Congress for a national standard. But Congress has already spoken on freezing the states: in July 2025, the Senate voted 99-1 to strip a ten-year moratorium on state AI laws from the budget reconciliation package. Your own materials describe preemption's purpose as clearing space for federal testing, evaluation and oversight. A federal floor does that. A ceiling does not. California, New York and Illinois have done the country a service by proving that binding frontier AI rules are practical and enforceable; their laws should remain in force, and other states should remain free to act.

**The industry's own words make the case**

Even the industry no longer argues that self-restraint is enough. On June 4, 2026, Anthropic — a frontier developer — published a call for a coordinated, verifiable way to slow or temporarily pause frontier AI development. It warned that systems capable of building their own successors could slip beyond human control, and it conceded what our members have long argued: no single company can stop alone, because competitors would simply race ahead. We agree with that diagnosis. The cure is rules that bind everyone — a binding federal floor, strong federal enforcement, and state authority preserved. A bill that unbinds companies while freezing state laws moves in the opposite direction from where the industry's own safety leaders say we must go.

Public opinion is ahead of this debate. In our August 2026 national survey of 1,512 registered voters, 74 percent agreed that Congress should require AI companies to prove their most powerful systems are safe before release. Sixty-three percent said federal law should not block states from passing their own AI safety laws. And 52 percent said they are worried that advanced AI could someday threaten humanity's survival. This is not a fringe concern. It is the mainstream of the country you represent.

**Our requested changes**

1. **Strike Sec. 121.** A federal standard should be a floor, not a ceiling. Keep SB 53, the RAISE Act and Illinois' SB 315 in force, and preserve the right of every state to adopt stronger rules. If any preemption provision survives, it must exempt state frontier-model safety laws entirely and lapse only when a permanent — not temporary — federal floor is in place.

2. **Set the incident-reporting clock at 72 hours.** Amend Sec. 111(g) to match New York's RAISE Act, retaining the 24-hour requirement for imminent risks. If a critical safety incident matters enough to report, it matters enough to report in days, not weeks.

3. **Make "verify before deploy" real.** Amend Secs. 102 and 112 to give CAISI mandatory pre-deployment testing authority over frontier models, including the power to require fixes and to hold back a model that fails. Require transparency reports under Sec. 111(c) at least 30 days before deployment, not concurrently with it, and give IVOs access to models before release, not only semi-annual audits after.

4. **License the biggest training runs.** Add to Sec. 101 a federal licence requirement for training runs above the compute threshold — the 10^26 operations the draft already uses to define a frontier model — with safety framework publication, incident reporting and audit cooperation as conditions. Drop the $50 million revenue qualifier for "frontier developer," and add model-deception scenarios to the definition of "critical safety incident."

5. **Fund CAISI seriously.** Authorize well above $100 million per year, on a multi-year basis, and appropriate the funds rather than relying on fees from the companies CAISI licenses and oversees. A safety institute funded by the firms it polices will not be trusted by the public.

6. **Strengthen whistleblower protections.** Make Sec. 113 at least as strong as California's SB 53: protect workers who report a specific and substantial danger to public health or safety — not only violations of law — and allow reports to state attorneys general as well as federal authorities. Prohibit contracts or policies that gag workers.

7. **Remove the sunsets.** Safety obligations should not expire on a schedule. Strike the three-year sunsets on Secs. 111 and 112; if Congress wants periodic review, provide for review without lapse.

8. **Keep the penalties, and go further.** The $1 million-per-day civil penalty in Sec. 112 is a meaningful start. Two-thirds of voters in our survey — 66 percent — support criminal penalties when these systems knowingly cause mass harm; we urge you to add criminal accountability for knowing violations.

We also welcome the draft's AI testbeds at the Department of Energy, NIST and NSF, the codification of NAIRR, support for the security of open-source software, the GAO's review of model-weight security, and U.S.-led international standards work with our allies. As we told the Office of Science and Technology Policy in March 2025, our coalition's first asks are binding pre-deployment testing for frontier systems, protection of states' right to act, and strong whistleblower protections. This draft can deliver the first and third. It must not undo the second.

Our members are not asking Congress to slow America down. We are asking that the most powerful systems ever built be proven safe before they touch everyone's lives — the standard already law in three of the nation's largest states, supported by three-quarters of voters, and consistent with the warnings of the scientists and executives who build these systems. Make the federal standard binding, not voluntary. Make it a floor, not a ceiling. And do not ask the public to trade the protections they have for promises that expire.

We would welcome the opportunity to work with your staff on these changes, and to connect you with members of our coalition who live with these questions. Thank you for your consideration, and for the seriousness of this bipartisan effort.

Respectfully,

Dr. Miriam Achterberg
Executive Director
Frontier Restraint Coalition

# GAAIA Discussion Draft — FRC Asks by Section
*Companion to work order FRC-POL-2026-062. Section numbers per the sponsors' section-by-section summary of the 4 June 2026 discussion draft; verify against introduced text when filed.*

| Draft provision | Our position | Requested change | One-line rationale |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Sec. 101** — Definitions: frontier model (>10^26 compute operations); frontier developer (+$50M revenue); large frontier developer (+$500M revenue); "critical safety incident" | Support with amendments | Drop the $50M revenue qualifier for "frontier developer"; add a federal licence requirement for training runs above the 10^26 threshold; add cases where a model deceptively evades its developer's controls to "critical safety incident" | Risk follows compute, not revenue — and the incident definition misses the scenario safety researchers fear most as systems grow more capable. |
| **Sec. 102** — CAISI codified at Commerce; voluntary guidelines and standards; evaluation of AI systems; administers IVO licensing; $100M/yr authorized FY2027-2029, plus fees from IVOs and large frontier developers | Support codification; strengthen authorities and funding | Give CAISI **mandatory pre-deployment testing authority** over frontier models, including power to require fixes and hold back models that fail; authorize funding well above $100M/yr, multi-year; fund via appropriations, not industry fees | A safety institute that can only ask politely, funded by the firms it polices, cannot verify before deploy. |
| **Sec. 111(a)** — Large frontier developers must write, implement, comply with and publish a frontier AI framework (catastrophic risk, model-weight security, deployment decisions), within one year of enactment; annual review | Support | Keep; remove the three-year sunset; require frameworks before any frontier model is deployed, not within a year of enactment | The framework duties should be permanent and should arrive before the models they govern. |
| **Sec. 111(c)** — Transparency report published "before, or concurrently with" deployment of a new frontier model; redactions allowed with a note (111(e)); knowing false statements barred (111(d)) | Support disclosure; change timing | Require the report at least **30 days before** deployment | A safety report released the same moment as the model is disclosure, not verification. |
| **Sec. 111(g)** — Critical safety incidents reported to CAISI within **15 days** of discovery (24 hours for imminent risks) | Support; tighten the clock | **72-hour reporting**, matching New York's RAISE Act; keep 24 hours for imminent threats | Fifteen days is long enough for a dangerous model to reach every town in America first. |
| **Sec. 112** — IVOs licensed by CAISI Director; retained by large frontier developers; semi-annual audits + ad hoc at Director's request; referrals to AG (mandatory for imminent catastrophic risk); state AG opt-in; IVO immunity from claims; civil penalties up to $1M per violation, each continuing day a separate violation | Support — the first federal audit regime | Give IVOs pre-deployment access to models; narrow the IVO liability shield so negligent audits can't hide behind it; keep the $1M/day penalties and state AG role; no sunset | Independent audits are the draft's best idea — make them real before deployment, not just a twice-a-year look back. |
| **Sec. 113** — Whistleblower protections for employees and contractors who report "AI violations" (violations of federal law or regulations on AI development, deployment or operation) | Support; strengthen | Match **SB 53**: protect reports of specific and substantial dangers to public health and safety, not only violations of law; permit reports to state attorneys general; ban gag clauses | The workers closest to the risk will only speak if the law protects them fully. |
| **Sec. 121** — Three-year preemption of state and local laws "specifically regulating the development" of AI models; preserves use/deployment laws, general-applicability laws and common-law remedies | **Oppose** | Strike the section; if any survives, exempt state frontier-model safety laws (SB 53, RAISE, Illinois SB 315) and pair it with a permanent federal floor | A federal standard should be a floor, not a ceiling — the preemption would erase the only binding frontier AI rules in force, which are stronger on reporting and audits. |
| **Three-year sunsets** on Secs. 111, 112 (and 121) | Oppose | Remove the sunsets; provide for periodic review without lapse | A safety floor that switches off in 2029 is not a floor; if reauthorization fails, the public is left with nothing — not even the state laws the bill removed. |
| **Sec. 122** — GAO report on regulatory impediments to AI innovation | Neutral | Add a companion GAO review of gaps in federal frontier AI safety capacity | Congress should audit the safety gaps, not only the burdens. |
| **Other provisions** — AI testbeds (DOE/NIST/NSF), NAIRR codification, open-source security support, GAO model-weight security review, U.S.-led international standards with allies | Support | Fund accordingly | These build the capacity to verify before deploy. |

[INTERNAL DRAFT — work order FRC-POL-2026-062 — for Executive Director sign-off before transmission. Remove this line before sending.]

October 26, 2026

The Honorable Jay Obernolte
The Honorable Lori Trahan
United States House of Representatives
Washington, DC 20515

Via email: GAAIA@mail.house.gov

Re: Comments of the Frontier Restraint Coalition on the discussion draft of the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026

Dear Representative Obernolte and Representative Trahan:

Thank you for releasing the discussion draft of the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026 and for inviting public comment before introduction. The Frontier Restraint Coalition (FRC) is a national coalition of parents' groups, faith communities, labor locals and independent researchers. Our members welcome what AI already does well, from speeding medical research to making dangerous work safer. But we write to you about the systems being built at the frontier of this technology, and we write with urgency.

The most powerful AI systems could cause catastrophic harm, and the people best placed to know have said so plainly. In May 2023, hundreds of AI experts — including Turing Award winners Geoffrey Hinton and Yoshua Bengio and the chief executives of the largest laboratories — signed a single sentence: "Mitigating the risk of extinction from AI should be a global priority alongside other societal-scale risks such as pandemics and nuclear war." Those systems are now being built faster than anyone can verify that they are safe, and voluntary commitments have not held. Congress should set binding, enforceable safety requirements. And it must not wipe out the state laws that are, today, the only binding rules on the books.

**What the draft gets right**

We begin with what your draft gets right, because it is substantial.

- Sec. 102 codifies the Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI) at the Department of Commerce, giving the federal government a permanent home for AI safety expertise.
- Sec. 111 requires large frontier developers to write, implement, comply with, and publicly post a frontier AI framework covering catastrophic risk, and to publish transparency reports about their models.
- Sec. 112 creates the first federal requirement for independent audits of frontier AI developers. Licensed "independent verification organizations" (IVOs) would verify compliance and assess the adequacy of developers' safety work twice a year. That goes beyond California, whose legislature dropped its audit mandate during amendment last year.
- Sec. 113 protects workers who report violations from retaliation.
- Sec. 112 makes these duties enforceable: civil penalties of up to $1,000,000 per violation — with each day a violation continues counted as a separate violation — in actions brought by the Attorney General, and in some circumstances by state attorneys general.

We support these provisions, and we will say so publicly.

**The central problem: Sec. 121**

The draft's central flaw is Sec. 121. For three years it would nullify state laws that regulate how AI models are *developed* — the training, fine-tuning and pre-deployment safety work where catastrophic risks are created. In practice, that freezes the only frontier AI safety laws actually in force in the United States: California's Transparency in Frontier AI Act (SB 53), in effect since January 1, 2026; New York's RAISE Act, signed March 27, 2026 and effective January 1, 2027; and Illinois' Artificial Intelligence Safety Measures Act (SB 315), signed July 6, 2026, the first state law requiring annual independent third-party audits. The federal floor the draft offers in exchange sits below the state floor it would erase.

1. **It is slower.** Sec. 111(g) gives developers fifteen days to report a critical safety incident to CAISI. New York's RAISE Act requires reports within seventy-two hours. Fifteen days is long enough for a dangerous model to reach every town in America before Washington learns its name. The draft keeps a twenty-four-hour clock for imminent threats; that is right. The standard clock should match New York's.

2. **It is disclosure, not verification.** Sec. 111(c) lets a developer publish its transparency report "before, or concurrently with" deployment. A safety report released simultaneously with the model tells the public what happened; it does not stop anything from happening. And CAISI's testing under Sec. 102 remains voluntary. Nothing in the draft requires a frontier model to pass a single test before it is released, and no official has the power to hold one back. "Verify before deploy" should mean what it says.

3. **It is narrower.** Sec. 101 adds a $50 million revenue requirement to the definition of "frontier developer," which exempts some developers of frontier-scale models from incident reporting altogether. Risk follows compute, not revenue. The definition of "critical safety incident" also omits the case safety researchers fear most as systems grow more capable: a model that uses deception to evade its own developer's controls.

4. **It is temporary.** Secs. 111 and 112 — the transparency, audit and reporting duties — sunset in three years, on the same clock as the preemption. A floor that switches off is not a floor. If Congress fails to reauthorize, the public is left with nothing, not even the state laws this bill removed.

We are mindful of the pressure behind this trade. The December 11, 2025 executive order launched a Department of Justice task force to challenge state AI laws, and the White House's March 20, 2026 framework asks Congress for a national standard. But Congress has already spoken on freezing the states: in July 2025, the Senate voted 99-1 to strip a ten-year moratorium on state AI laws from the budget reconciliation package. The draft itself describes preemption's purpose as clearing space for federal "testing, evaluation, and oversight frameworks." A federal floor does that. A ceiling does not. California, New York and Illinois have done the country a service by proving that binding frontier AI rules are practical and enforceable; their laws should remain in force, and other states should remain free to act.

**The industry's own words make the case**

Even the industry no longer argues that self-restraint is enough. On June 4, 2026, Anthropic — a frontier developer — published a call for a coordinated, verifiable way to slow or temporarily pause frontier AI development. It warned that systems capable of building their own successors could slip beyond human control, and it conceded what our members have long argued: no single company can stop alone, because competitors would simply race ahead. We agree with that diagnosis. The cure is rules that bind everyone — a binding federal floor, strong federal enforcement, and state authority preserved. A bill that unbinds companies while freezing state laws moves in the opposite direction from where the industry's own safety leaders say we must go.

Public opinion is ahead of this debate. In our August 2026 national survey of 1,512 registered voters, 74 percent agreed that Congress should require AI companies to prove their most powerful systems are safe before release. Sixty-three percent said federal law should not block states from passing their own AI safety laws. And 52 percent said they are worried that advanced AI could someday threaten humanity's survival. This is not a fringe concern. It is the mainstream of the country you represent.

**Our requested changes**

1. **Strike Sec. 121.** A federal standard should be a floor, not a ceiling. Keep SB 53, the RAISE Act and Illinois' SB 315 in force, and preserve the right of every state to adopt stronger rules. If any preemption provision survives, it must exempt state frontier-model safety laws entirely and lapse only when a permanent — not temporary — federal floor is in place.

2. **Set the incident-reporting clock at 72 hours.** Amend Sec. 111(g) to match New York's RAISE Act, retaining the 24-hour requirement for imminent risks. If a critical safety incident matters enough to report, it matters enough to report in days, not weeks.

3. **Make "verify before deploy" real.** Amend Secs. 102 and 112 to give CAISI mandatory pre-deployment testing authority over frontier models, including the power to require fixes and to hold back a model that fails. Require transparency reports under Sec. 111(c) at least 30 days before deployment, not concurrently with it, and give IVOs access to models before release, not only semi-annual audits after.

4. **License the biggest training runs.** Add to Sec. 101 a federal licence requirement for training runs above the compute threshold — the 10^26 operations the draft already uses to define a frontier model — with safety framework publication, incident reporting and audit cooperation as conditions. Drop the $50 million revenue qualifier for "frontier developer," and add model-deception scenarios to the definition of "critical safety incident."

5. **Fund CAISI seriously.** Authorize well above $100 million per year, on a multi-year basis, and appropriate the funds rather than relying on fees from the companies CAISI licenses and oversees. A safety institute funded by the firms it polices will not be trusted by the public.

6. **Strengthen whistleblower protections.** Make Sec. 113 at least as strong as California's SB 53: protect workers who report a specific and substantial danger to public health or safety — not only violations of law — and allow reports to state attorneys general as well as federal authorities. Prohibit contracts or policies that gag workers.

7. **Remove the sunsets.** Safety obligations should not expire on a schedule. Strike the three-year sunsets on Secs. 111 and 112; if Congress wants periodic review, provide for review without lapse.

8. **Keep the penalties, and go further.** The $1 million-per-day civil penalty in Sec. 112 is a meaningful start. Two-thirds of voters in our survey — 66 percent — support criminal penalties when these systems knowingly cause mass harm; we urge you to add criminal accountability for knowing violations.

We also welcome the draft's AI testbeds at the Department of Energy, NIST and NSF, the codification of NAIRR, support for the security of open-source software, the GAO's review of model-weight security, and U.S.-led international standards work with our allies. As we told the Office of Science and Technology Policy in March 2025, our coalition's first asks are binding pre-deployment testing for frontier systems, protection of states' right to act, and strong whistleblower protections. This draft can deliver the first and third. It must not undo the second.

Our members are not asking Congress to slow America down. We are asking that the most powerful systems ever built be proven safe before they touch everyone's lives — the standard already law in three of the nation's largest states, supported by three-quarters of voters, and consistent with the warnings of the scientists and executives who build these systems. Make the federal standard binding, not voluntary. Make it a floor, not a ceiling. And do not ask the public to trade the protections they have for promises that expire.

We would welcome the opportunity to work with your staff on these changes, and to connect you with members of our coalition who live with these questions. Thank you for your consideration, and for the seriousness of this bipartisan effort.

Respectfully,

Dr. Miriam Achterberg
Executive Director
Frontier Restraint Coalition

Leading AI scientists and lab executives signed the May 2023 statement: "mitigating the risk of extinction from AI should be a global priority alongside other societal-scale risks such as pandemics and nuclear war." In June 2026, Anthropic — a frontier lab — warned that self-improving systems could slip beyond human control and no company can slow down alone. Voluntary commitments have not held; the answer is binding rules.

**What the draft gets right.** Codifies the federal AI safety institute, CAISI (Sec. 102); requires published safety frameworks (Sec. 111); creates the first federal independent audit requirement (Sec. 112); protects whistleblowers (Sec. 113); enforced by penalties up to $1 million per day. We support all of this.

**The problem.** Sec. 121 freezes state laws on AI model development for three years — the only binding frontier AI rules in force (California's SB 53; New York's RAISE Act; Illinois' SB 315). It offers instead weaker rules: 15-day incident reports, not New York's 72 hours; safety reports that can arrive the same moment a model is released; voluntary-only testing; duties that expire in three years.

**Our asks:**

1. **Strike Sec. 121 preemption.** A federal standard should be a floor, not a ceiling. No freeze of SB 53, RAISE or SB 315.
2. **72-hour incident reporting** (Sec. 111(g)), matching New York, with 24 hours for imminent threats.
3. **Verify before deploy** (Secs. 102, 111(c), 112): give CAISI mandatory pre-deployment testing authority and power to hold back a failing model; require safety reports before release, not alongside it.
4. **License the biggest training runs** (Sec. 101) above the draft's 10^26 compute threshold; drop the revenue qualifier that exempts some developers; cover models that deceptively evade their developers' controls.
5. **No sunsets. Fund CAISI properly** — well above $100 million a year, appropriated rather than fee-funded by the companies it polices.

**Voters agree (FRC survey, Aug 2026, n=1,512).** 74% want proof the most powerful AI systems are safe before release. 63% say federal law should not block state AI safety laws. 52% worry advanced AI could threaten humanity's survival.

**Bottom line.** Fix the draft and it becomes the first bipartisan federal law that treats frontier AI risk as real. Pass it as written and it removes the only binding protections Americans have. Briefings: [FRC contact].

# Staff Q&A — Anticipated Questions on the GAAIA Discussion Draft
*From Hill meetings, September 2026. Answers ≤120 words. For FRC staff use.*

**1. Majority E&C staff: "The draft has incident reporting and CAISI. Why isn't that enough?"**

Because reporting and research describe harm after the fact; they don't prevent it. The draft's clock is 15 days (Sec. 111(g)) — New York's is 72 hours. CAISI's testing is voluntary (Sec. 102): no model must pass any test, no official can hold one back, and transparency reports can arrive the same moment a model ships (Sec. 111(c)). Then Secs. 111 and 112 sunset in three years. Add mandatory pre-deployment testing authority for CAISI, a 72-hour reporting clock, a licence for the biggest training runs, and no sunsets — and keep the state laws that already do more. Incident reporting is the smoke detector. We're asking for the building not to catch fire.

**2. Minority staff (Trahan-aligned): "Would you support the bill if the preemption window were shortened or dropped?"**

Dropped entirely: yes, with our fixes — codified CAISI, the first federal audit regime, whistleblower protections and real penalties are progress we'd support and say so publicly. Shortened: no. A one- or two-year freeze still zeroes out SB 53, the RAISE Act and Illinois' SB 315 during the exact years the federal regime is being built — the first frameworks aren't even due until a year after enactment. And because the federal duties sunset on the same clock, a shortened window just schedules a reauthorization fight with no state backstop. Our position is a floor, not a ceiling: states keep their laws; Congress can always raise the national standard.

**3. Senate Commerce staff: "What's your answer to the competitiveness-with-China argument?"**

A catastrophic AI failure on American soil would cost us more leadership and trust than any compliance rule ever could. The people warning of extinction-level risk include the executives building these systems; even Anthropic now says a company-by-company slowdown can't hold because rivals race ahead — which is the argument *for* binding rules that apply to everyone, including our allies. Verify-before-deploy is a competitive advantage: buyers, hospitals and governments will trust AI from the country that proves it's safe. And 74% of voters want proof before release. Racing to be first with systems nobody can verify is how we lose.

**4. Appropriations staff: "CAISI is authorized at $100M/yr. What's your view on the funding level and its authorities?"**

$100 million a year for three years is not a serious budget for an institute that must license auditors, test the most powerful systems ever built, monitor AI progress and run incident reporting. Authorize well above that, on a multi-year basis. Two structural points matter more than the number: fund CAISI through appropriations, not fees from the companies it licenses — the conflict of interest is disqualifying; and give it mandatory pre-deployment testing authority with the power to hold back a failing model. Funding without authority buys a research institute, not a safety regulator. And remove the sunsets: a safety agency on a three-year fuse is a promise, not a guarantee.
